{"id": "19:33/q05", "question": "What protection does the peace grant at birth, death and resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q05/p1", "position": "God's safety covers Jesus at all three stages, with differing explanations of each danger.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā take the days as birth, death and resurrection; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qāḍī and others describe protection across them. Al-Kalbī maps them to worldly life, grave and resurrection. Al-Ṭabarī specifies Satan, death's terror and Resurrection fear; al-Baghawī says Satan's piercing, shirk and resurrection terrors; al-Bursawī adds death's hardships and Hell. Al-Wāḥidī cites the prophetic report that Satan touches newborns except Jesus, a barrier intervening. Ibn al-Jawzī and Study Quran transmit birth protection; Study Quran adds grave trials for John and Jesus' fearless death after his return and resurrection with humanity, citing 43:61 and 4:157–159. Muqātil's second gloss gives fatherless creation, grave pressure and proof against those calling Jesus Lord. Al-Māwardī reports an alternative with Satan's poke and no grave pressure because Jesus was not buried; he finds its resurrection gloss unsatisfactory and suggests no reckoning after God cleared Jesus of sin. Al-Qushayrī specifies protection from Christian excess and Jewish disparagement at birth and trials outside divine union later. Al-Biqāʿī notes Satan did not harm his birth."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q06", "question": "Why are these three days singled out?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q06/p1", "position": "They are the three vulnerable turning points at which a person especially needs divine mercy or peace.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says these are moments of special need for mercy; al-Qāḍī calls them the most vulnerable moments and connects Jesus' request to John's peace. Al-Shaʿbī calls them three moments of human frailty; al-Riḍā calls them the most frightening moments for John and Jesus. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls them the comprehensive turning points of Jesus' existence and says the wording applies peace throughout his life."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q07", "question": "What does Jesus' reference to birth, death and resurrection establish about him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q07/p1", "position": "Jesus is a created human servant who was born, will die and will be raised.", "reasons": "Wahb says Jesus' words disclose that he had no father, would die and would rise alive, connecting this to 19:34. Ibn Kathīr says he shares creatures' life, death and raising, while God protects him at the hardest moments. Al-Biqāʿī says birth and resurrection show his humanity. Iṣlāḥī parallels John and rejects weak reports and contrary claims as unable to override these stages. Kuranyolu connects his birth, death and rising with his earlier claim to be God's servant and prophet rather than deity or part of a trinity; his duty of worship also implies prayer among post-Abrahamic prophets despite differing forms. Its passage summary adds blessing everywhere, respect for Mary, and freedom from tyranny and disobedience."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q08", "question": "What bearing does Jesus' stated death have on predestination?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q08/p1", "position": "It states his decreed course through death and troubles adherents of predestination.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Mālik's observation that this verse is difficult for adherents of predestination because Jesus declares this fixed course."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q09", "question": "Does being raised alive exclude life in the grave?", "turns_on": "Whether 'alive' specifies the final embodied state or denies intermediate life altogether.", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q09/p1", "position": "It implies no life in the grave.", "reasons": "An objection quoted by al-Bursawī reads the resurrection phrase as proof against grave life."}, {"id": "19:33/q09/p2", "position": "It describes everlasting embodied resurrection life; intermediate spirit life still exists.", "reasons": "The answer in al-Bursawī distinguishes enduring resurrection life from grave life; he explains barzakh as life of spirit alone, resurrection as spirit joined to body, and says spirits do not cease living after creation."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q10", "question": "What does yawm mean in these phrases?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q10/p1", "position": "A time or occasion.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī cites birth, death and resurrection alongside travel, residence and harvest as occasions described by yawm."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q11", "question": "How do the three day phrases function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q11/p1", "position": "They are temporal adverbials governed by the predicate's implied stability in 'upon me'.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī calls the days adverbials governed by the predicate. Al-Samīn locates their governor in the implied stability of ʿalayya and rejects dependence on al-salām because it would separate a verbal noun from its complement."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q12", "question": "How is wulidtu read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q12/p1", "position": "Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads a past verb referring to Mary, with feminine tāʾ.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān describes yawma wulidtu as 'the day I was born'; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī specify an active waladtu with feminine tāʾ agreeing with Jesus' mother. Their descriptions of the verb's form vary."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q13", "question": "What does being raised alive denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q13/p1", "position": "Life after death on Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī explains ḥayāt as life after death, comparing 46:33 and 75:40 on God's reviving the dead. Muqātil likewise places the raising alive in the Hereafter; Yaḥyā identifies it with Resurrection Day."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q14", "question": "What is the grammatical role of ḥayyan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q14/p1", "position": "It is a confirmatory circumstantial accusative reinforcing the already implied state.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls ḥayyan emphatic. {"id": "19:33/q15", "question": "When did Jesus speak these words, and what followed?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported infant speech is historical speech of these words or a projection of mature teaching; one report also distinguishes womb speech from glorification.", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q15/p1", "position": "He spoke miraculously as an infant, then fell silent until ordinary speaking age.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the speech ended and Jesus developed like other children; al-Naḥḥās calls speech in Mary's lap the sign. Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Māwardī, Ibn ʿAbbās and exegetes in al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī and Study Quran report silence until boyhood or normal speech age. Study Quran calls the infant ability temporary."}, {"id": "19:33/q15/p2", "position": "The passage may present future maturity as past speech, or Jesus may have uttered it after maturity.", "reasons": "Asad reads the past tense in 30–33 as a trope projecting a later truth despite 3:46's cradle-speech wording. He considers revelation and prophethood before full intellectual and experiential maturity inconceivable. He also reports the alternative that the whole passage was said after maturity as a summary of Jesus' ethics and servant identity."}, {"id": "19:33/q15/p3", "position": "Jesus glorified God in the womb when others were present, though Mary heard him speak to her alone.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's report in al-Durr distinguishes Jesus' speech to Mary from his glorification before other people while still in her womb."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q16", "question": "What did Jesus' speech establish for Mary and the onlookers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q16/p1", "position": "It vindicated Mary's chastity and showed Jesus' servant and messenger status.", "reasons": "Muqātil says his naming his mother but no father prompted Zechariah to embrace him and testify he was God's servant and messenger. Al-Baghawī says people recognized Mary's innocence; al-Ṭabrisī reports the same purpose, and al-Bursawī says they knew she was chaste and innocent."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q17", "question": "Why was the infant-speech sign not given to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q17/p1", "position": "His people might have confused it with soothsaying.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī gives this reason and mentions other wonders involving speech by infants, animals and inanimate things."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q18", "question": "How does Jesus' greeting relate to John's?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q18/p1", "position": "It parallels John's peace at the same three stages, though the wording and speaker differ.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī link it to 19:15; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Qāshānī, al-Bursawī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Iṣlāḥī and Study Quran likewise mark the parallel. Al-Qāshānī grounds it in Jesus' sanctified abstract essence, unhidden by matter even in childhood. Al-Bursawī says John received the same protections. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes John's indefinite divine greeting versus Jesus' definite self-greeting. Al-Bursawī's sheikh contrasts third and first person while crediting both with annihilation and completeness."}]}

{"id": "19:33/q20", "question": "Where was the surah revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q20/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, with a reported exception for the prostration verse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this surah Meccan like its predecessor and reports Muqātil's view that its prostration verse was revealed in Medina after the migration to Abyssinia."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q21", "question": "What may Jesus' self-description of praiseworthy qualities teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q21/p1", "position": "One may state praiseworthy qualities to inform others if it is not boasting.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī derives this permission from Jesus' self-description."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q22", "question": "What does the count of Jesus' speech suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q22/p1", "position": "Its thirty-three words match a proposed lifespan of thirty-three years.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān counts from 'qāla innī ʿabd Allāh' through 'ubʿathu ḥayyan' and reports this inference about Jesus' lifespan."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q23", "question": "What inward reading is given to Jesus and his peace?", "turns_on": "Different inward referents: a sanctified essence free of material defects or spiritual meaning threatened by the ego.", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q23/p1", "position": "Peace frees a sanctified essence from defects of attachment to matter.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says Jesus shares John's peace because his abstract essence remains unhidden by matter even in childhood; he glosses peace as freedom from defects produced by material attachment."}, {"id": "19:33/q23/p2", "position": "Jesus symbolizes a meaning born of divine breath in the heart that can still die under egoic traits and practices.", "reasons": "The Najmī taʾwīl reported by al-Bursawī says even someone spiritually alive should not presume immunity from overpowering ego traits and practices."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q24", "question": "What further reports about Jesus and John accompany the verse?", "turns_on": "The reports recount different events rather than competing versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q24/p1", "position": "Jesus redirected praise from his mother to people who read, follow and practice God's Book.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Qatāda's account of a woman's blessing on Jesus' womb and nursing mother and Jesus' reply."}, {"id": "19:33/q24/p2", "position": "John warned against security from God's plan, and Jesus against despair of His mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports a prophetic saying that God loved the one of them with the better expectation of Him."}, {"id": "19:33/q24/p3", "position": "John and Jesus each attained perfection in different stations.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports John's blood boiling until seventy thousand were killed in retaliation, whereas Jesus was raised to the highest heaven, manifesting beauty."}, {"id": "19:33/q24/p4", "position": "One chronology gives Mary's age and Jesus' prophetic and earthly milestones.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī's Takmila dates Jesus' birth to the Successor kings, Mary's age then to thirteen, Jesus' prophethood to thirty and raising to thirty-three, and Mary's life for six more years."}, {"id": "19:33/q24/p5", "position": "Mary took Jesus to Egypt with Joseph to escape Herod.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī's Takmila adds that Persian envoys came because of a star and an angel warned them not to inform Herod."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q25", "question": "What does the cited Arabic ellipsis excursus illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q25/p1", "position": "Arabic omits complements or nouns recoverable from context.", "reasons": "Sībawayh explains an understood dhāk after laysa ghayr and laysa illā for brevity; an understood al-wāḥid after min is supported by common speech, 4:159 and poetry. He interprets mā al-dahr illā tāratān as one turn bringing death and the other hard-won life, comparing omission after ghayr with deletion of part of a compound name."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q26", "question": "What does the cited proper-name excursus explain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q26/p1", "position": "Names identify particular individuals and take several forms, with rules for titles and kunyas.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says specific rulings require individual identification, and humans have more distinct individual needs than other animals. He divides names into personal names, titles and kunyas, citing Ibrāhīm, Isrāʾīl and Abū Lahab; Sībawayh's animal examples show name plus kunya, name alone and kunya alone. Al-Rāzī lists kunyas formed from father, mother, son or daughter; unknown or known lineage, including camel-age names Ibn/Bint Makhāḍ and Labūn; joining unannexed names to titles but keeping annexed names separate; and motives of fact, hope, opposite meaning, reciprocal father-son naming or a notable trait."}]}
{"id": "19:33/q27", "question": "How can indefinite salām begin a sentence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:33/q27/p1", "position": "Its frequent use and generic sense make it sufficiently definite in effect to begin a sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says this greeting is frequent and generic nouns can nearly convey the benefit of definiteness; al-Ṭabrisī gives the same explanation."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q01", "question": "What does Abraham's “peace be upon you” mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether salām functions as assurance, farewell, formal greeting, forbearance, or a prayer; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contests a farewell because departure came later.", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q01/p1", "position": "He assures his father of safety from harm or insult at his hands.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Qurṭubī say Abraham had no command to fight his father for unbelief. Al-Biqāʿī qualifies the assurance by any contrary divine command. Ibn Kathīr grounds it in filial respect. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links the assurance to the threat, the promised prayer, and his later withdrawal; Study Quran says it ends confrontation without fighting. Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī include refraining from hurtful speech."}, {"id": "19:47/q01/p2", "position": "It is a peaceful farewell and separation from his father.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr says he leaves because of unbelief. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī compare 28:55 and 25:63. Al-Bayḍāwī calls it kindness in reply to injury; al-Nasafī allows conciliatory parting. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the farewell comes first to show no resentment at leaving for God. Iṣlāḥī says salām serves as an affectionate farewell formula. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that actual departure occurred later."}, {"id": "19:47/q01/p3", "position": "It is a courteous greeting that answers his father's harshness with filial kindness.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī stresses his father's status and past upbringing, and prefers this to a mere farewell. Al-Ṭabrisī says Abraham leaves without disobedience. Abū Ḥayyān calls it filial duty; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes kindness at their last encounter. Iṣlāḥī notes salām is also a blessed greeting on meeting."}, {"id": "19:47/q01/p4", "position": "It is a forbearing reply to ignorant or abusive speech.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī calls it a good response and al-Ḥasan a word of forbearance. Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir compares 25:63 after the father's idolatrous invitation and threat; al-Naqqāsh calls Abraham the forbearing man addressing a fool. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Study Quran also cite the peaceful reply to ignorance; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds 25:72."}, {"id": "19:47/q01/p5", "position": "He prays for his father's safety to win him over.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī infer conciliatory prayer from the immediately following promise to seek forgiveness."}, {"id": "19:47/q01/p6", "position": "In an inward reading, peace asks God to remove the father's material veils.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says his father's essence lies hidden behind material veils."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q02", "question": "What does salām mean in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "These are distinct Arabic uses of the word; the notes apply safety to this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q02/p1", "position": "Safety or release from harm, including a prayer for safety.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj lists the verbal noun of salima and a plural of salāmah; as a prayer it seeks safety in religion, person, and property. He explains reconciliation as safety from evil, stones called salām for hardness, and a ladder carrying one to safety or a desired place. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes it as safety, with ʿalā picturing its establishment, and compares 19:15."}, {"id": "19:47/q02/p2", "position": "As a divine name, al-Salām names the possessor of peace and safety.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says God owns safety understood as release from harm."}, {"id": "19:47/q02/p3", "position": "Salām also names a large, strong tree.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj lists the tree; Ibn al-Jawzī suggests its name reflects freedom from afflictions."}, {"id": "19:47/q02/p4", "position": "Salām can mean goodness.", "reasons": "Some interpreters give this fourth sense; Ibn Qutayba applies it to the salām of the Night of Decree."}]}

nd parting, like the greeting of the ignorant. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is specified and can convey the sense of an accusative 'I greet you peacefully,' citing Sibawayh's fierce beast example. Al-Qurṭubī says its restriction and definite complement license the indefinite subject. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī parse it as a nominal sentence or noun. Sibawayh says adding lā to an already governed invocation noun preserves its nominal form; lā salām ʿalayka and Jarīr's lā salām ʿalā ʿAmr parallel the verbal prayer lā sallama Allāhu ʿalayhi. He supports the nominal pattern by the corresponding verbal construction and notes that no imperative lā iḍrib is available."}, {"id": "19:47/q03/p2", "position": "An accusative salāman is an absolute verbal noun expressing a prayer for safety.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān treats it as a verbal noun and conciliatory address; al-Ālūsī calls it an absolute verbal noun. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says even nominative salāmun carries the sense of an accusative peaceful greeting."}, {"id": "19:47/q03/p3", "position": "Related nominal invocation and lā constructions retain or change case according to their particular function.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says lā bika al-sūʾ prays 'may God not harm you'; lā enters wishing and welcome formulas as in verbal equivalents. Lā sawāʾ and lāhā Allāhi dhā replace a prior predicate; lā nawlaka substitutes for lā yanbaghī; bi-lā dhanb means 'without'; lā shayʾ diminishes a matter. In ḥīna lā ḥīn, lā is null; lā barāḥ and lā mustaṣrikh are commonly accusative but may be nominative. A bare predicate lā fāris is awkward without a contrast, although a Banū Sulūl poem attests bare lā nafʿ. Lā governs questions as statements, illustrated by Ḥassān. With wish meaning, interrogative alif plus lā governs accusative without nunation; the form is not nominative because it neither answers a question nor means laysa. In alā māʾan wa-labanan bāridan ḥulwan each adjective qualifies a separate noun, and alā ghulāman afḍala minka is an accusative wish for a boy without a predicate."}, {"id": "19:47/q03/p4", "position": "Alā rajulan can be a rhetorical prompt rather than a wish.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl paraphrases it as 'Do you not show me a man whom God rewarded well?' Sibawayh presents this reading."}, {"id": "19:47/q03/p5", "position": "The nunation in alā rajulan can be poetic necessity.", "reasons": "Yūnus supplies this alternative; Sibawayh calls it possible while presenting al-Khalīl's prompt reading for others."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q04", "question": "What variant readings affect salām?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q04/p1", "position": "Abū al-Barhasm reads salāman in the accusative.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya records the reading; al-Samīn refers its parsing to his earlier analysis."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q05", "question": "May one initiate salām to a non-Muslim, and what does this verse imply?", "turns_on": "Whether Abraham's salām is a prescribed greeting or only peaceful disengagement, and how reports forbidding first greetings relate to need, mixed company, and 60:8.", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q05/p1", "position": "One may initiate such a greeting, at least to a non-hostile unbeliever.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī report this from those who take Abraham's words as a real greeting. Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna cites 60:8 and 60:4; al-Qurṭubī prefers his reading. Abū Usāma greeted all passersby because Muslims are told to spread salām. Al-Awzāʿī says greeting and withholding it both have righteous precedent. The permissive report contrasts with a prohibitive report, which al-Ṭabarī treats as general and specific. Al-Ālūsī reports the view but rejects its proofs."}, {"id": "19:47/q05/p2", "position": "An initial greeting is prohibited without a qualifying reason.", "reasons": "The stricter report says greeting honors unbelievers; Anas calls salām the greeting of Paradise. The majority reading makes Abraham's words peaceful disengagement, not a salutation. Abū Hurayra's sound report forbids first greeting Jews and Christians and directs road precedence. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī say this report outweighs the verse as a prooftext for permission. Al-Qurṭubī confines prohibition to cases with no need or social right."}, {"id": "19:47/q05/p3", "position": "An initial greeting is permitted for need, companionship, neighborly right, travel, or a mixed gathering.", "reasons": "Al-Nakhaʿī allows it for a need involving a Jew or Christian. Al-Qurṭubī lists need, companionship, neighborhood, and travel; Ibn Masʿūd greeted a Persian travel companion because companionship has a right. Al-Ḥasan permits greeting a mixed gathering, and the report of Usāma says the Prophet greeted a mixed gathering before Badr."}, {"id": "19:47/q05/p4", "position": "Greeting a non-Muslim is permitted in wartime but not in peace.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna's formulation with 60:8 and 60:4; he says Abraham's example excludes asking forgiveness, not greeting. This wording differs from the non-hostile formulation reported by al-Qurṭubī."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q06", "question": "What conduct does Abraham's reply teach toward a harsh or obstinate person?", "turns_on": "The notes give an ethical reading and a mystical application.", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q06/p1", "position": "Answer abuse gently while fulfilling filial duty, then leave an unreceptive person peacefully.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says Abraham replied from settled insight while retaining hope after a threat. Al-Rāzī and al-Bursawī infer departure after fruitless advice and kindness toward abuse. Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress filial duty and forbearance. Ibn Ṭāhir says 25:63 supports shunning wicked people for religion; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls peaceful reply generous conduct. Iṣlāḥī says the promise shows tenderness and love despite callousness."}, {"id": "19:47/q06/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, the peace marks turning from worldly others while remaining gentle to the ignorant.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records this mystical application."}]}
{"id": "19:47/q07", "question": "What does Abraham promise by 'I shall ask forgiveness for you'?", "turns_on": "Whether forgiveness is sought through future faith, under an unstated condition, in hope before prohibition or final enmity is known, or only as relief from worldly punishment; 9:114, 60:4, and 26:86 are central.", "positions": [{"id": "19:47/q07/p1", "position": "He will ask God to guide his father to faith and repentance, through which forgiveness becomes possible.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr make guidance a prerequisite. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers it to supposing forgiveness of persistent unbelief.
